common_name: Solomone Yellow Clivia (California Yellow Bush Lily Strain)

planting.note: Plant tissue-cultured or division-grown offsets in deep shade in humus-rich, well-drained soil; 'Solomone Yellow' was selected and mass-propagated by grower Joe Solomone of Watsonville, California, and remains one of the most widely distributed yellow clivia strains in the US nursery trade.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to deep shade, keeping the fleshy roots somewhat crowded in their container for the most reliable flowering. 'Solomone Yellow' bears large, creamy to butter-yellow, tubular flowers in dense rounded umbels above broad, strap-shaped, dark green leaves, and unlike many rarer yellow selections it has been propagated at commercial volume for decades, making it one of the more affordable yellow clivia options for US collectors. Give plants a cool, dry rest of six to eight weeks in winter with minimal water to set flower buds, then resume regular watering once a bloom stalk emerges from the leaf axils. Divide only when a clump becomes tightly congested, since flowering slows for a season or two after roots are disturbed.

common_name: Kirstenbosch Yellow Clivia (Fragrant Group 1 Yellow Strain)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown offsets in deep shade in rich, well-drained soil; 'Kirstenbosch Yellow' was bred at Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden in Cape Town and belongs to a true-breeding yellow line, so seedlings raised from self- or sib-pollination stay reliably yellow.

directions: Site in deep, even shade in humus-rich, sharply drained soil, since this slower-growing strain resents soggy roots more than most clivia selections. 'Kirstenbosch Yellow' carries light, fairly broad leaves and produces well-reflexed, pale yellow flowers with a deeper yellow throat in early autumn to spring depending on climate, along with an unusual sweet fragrance often compared to azalea blossoms, and its fruit ripens bright yellow rather than the typical orange-red. Because the strain breeds true from seed within its own line, it is a good choice for collectors wanting to raise their own true-yellow seedlings rather than relying only on division. Give plants a dry, cool winter rest of several weeks before the bloom period to encourage a strong flush of flower stalks.
sources: South African National Biodiversity Institute — PlantZAfrica

common_name: Chubb's Peach Clivia (Apricot-Blushed Yellow Bush Lily)

planting.note: Plant division-grown offsets in deep shade in rich, well-drained soil; 'Chubb Peach' is a South African seed strain foundational to modern peach and apricot clivia breeding, and since it is grown from seed, individual plants vary somewhat in the depth of peach blush over the base yellow.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to deep shade, allowing the clump to become moderately pot-bound before expecting heavy bloom. 'Chubb Peach' produces umbels of soft, apricot-flushed flowers over an essentially yellow ground color, a pastel departure from the orange-red of species-type clivia, carried above the same broad, leathery, strap-shaped evergreen leaves. As a seed-propagated strain rather than a single cloned cultivar, plants sold under this name show a natural range from pale blush to more pronounced peach, and growers seeking the deepest color should select flowering-size plants in bloom rather than buying by name alone. A cool, dry winter rest of six to eight weeks with reduced watering encourages the strongest spring flowering.

common_name: Sahin Twin Red Clivia (Dwarf Twin-Flowered Bush Lily)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in deep shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; 'Sahin Twin Red' is a compact Dutch-bred selection out of Belgian Hybrid stock, notable for reliably sending up two bloom stalks per growth instead of the usual single scape.

directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light in humus-rich, well-drained soil, keeping the clump slightly pot-bound to promote flowering. 'Sahin Twin Red' is a dwarfed selection from Belgian Hybrid Clivia miniata breeding lines, staying noticeably more compact than typical florist strains while producing dark orange-red flowers that deepen in color as they age, and it is distinctive for regularly throwing a paired second flower stalk from the same growth. Its smaller stature makes it easier to manage on a windowsill or in a small pot than full-size Belgian Hybrids, though it still needs the same six-to-eight-week cool, dry winter rest to trigger strong spring bloom. Divide congested offsets in spring only when necessary, since disturbance can delay flowering for a season.
